title: "Audit 13: where the correlation between ions comes from"
author: "Jannik Franken"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true

## Purpose

After fitting the contrasts' models, ions remain correlated with each other
about twice as much as independent ions would be (analysis/08, section 6).
Set tests then disagree strongly: camera, which accounts for the correlation,
finds no significant set, while ULM, which assumes independent ions, finds
hundreds. A correlation that runs through all ions usually points to a global
factor per line (amount of material, overall signal, ion suppression). This
notebook checks whether such a factor exists, whether one covariate removes it,
and what that does to the positive control.

**Decision supported:** whether a per-line covariate enters all models, and
how the enrichment is reported.

## Inputs

- `data/derived/cancer-cell-lines/shorthouse_v1/shorthouse_analysis_v1.rds`
- `data/derived/cancer-cell-lines/shorthouse_v1/06_ion_sets.tsv`, `06_sets.tsv`
- `config.yml`: `differential.contrasts.nrf2_lung`, `enrichment`

## Methods

A baseline model `~ batch + tissue` was fitted with limma to the log2 values of
all lines used in models. Its residuals were analysed with a PCA (ions
centred, not scaled). A global factor shows up as a leading component that
explains more variance than expected for unstructured noise, and whose
loadings have the same sign for most ions. The expectation for noise was
obtained by fitting the same model to data with the line labels permuted
within each ion, which keeps every ion's distribution but removes all
correlation between ions.

Two candidate covariates were compared:

- the **median log2 intensity of the line** over all ions, a standard
  normalisation factor;
- the **first principal component of the residuals**, which captures the
  global factor directly but may also absorb biological signal.

For each, the median absolute correlation between ions after the model, the
positive control (NRF2 in lung lines, analysis/05) and the camera test of the
glutathione sets (analysis/08) were recomputed.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

source(here::here("analyses/cancer-cell-lines/R/use_case.R"))
source(here::here("analyses/cancer-cell-lines/R/plotting.R"))
source(here::here("analyses/cancer-cell-lines/R/mutations.R"))
source(here::here("analyses/cancer-cell-lines/R/differential.R"))
config <- load_config()
derived_dir <- uc_dir(config, "derived")
fig_dir <- uc_dir(config, "output", "audit_13_ion_correlation")
set.seed(config$contrast$seed)

data <- readRDS(file.path(derived_dir, "shorthouse_analysis_v1.rds"))
lines <- filter(data$lines, in_models)
y <- t(data$log2[lines$line, ])   # ions x lines

# median absolute correlation between ions of a residual matrix (ions x lines)
median_abs_cor <- function(residual) {
    m <- cor(t(residual))
    median(abs(m[upper.tri(m)]))
}
```

## 1. Residual structure of the baseline model

```{r baseline}
X0 <- model.matrix(~ batch + tissue, data = lines)
residual0 <- residuals(limma::lmFit(y, X0), y)

# the same model on permuted data: each ion's values shuffled across lines
y_perm <- t(apply(y, 1, sample))
residual_perm <- residuals(limma::lmFit(y_perm, X0), y_perm)

pc0 <- prcomp(t(residual0), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
pc_perm <- prcomp(t(residual_perm), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
share <- tibble(component = 1:10,
                observed = (pc0$sdev^2 / sum(pc0$sdev^2))[1:10],
                permuted = (pc_perm$sdev^2 / sum(pc_perm$sdev^2))[1:10])
share %>% mutate(across(c(observed, permuted), ~ round(.x, 3)))

c(median_abs_correlation = round(median_abs_cor(residual0), 3),
  median_abs_correlation_permuted = round(median_abs_cor(residual_perm), 3),
  share_of_ions_with_positive_PC1_loading = round(mean(pc0$rotation[, 1] > 0), 2))
```

```{r scree, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- share %>%
    pivot_longer(-component, names_to = "data", values_to = "share") %>%
    ggplot(aes(component, share, colour = data)) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = uc_palette(c("observed", "permuted"))) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
    labs(x = "Component of the residuals", y = "Share of residual variance", colour = NULL,
         title = "Residual structure after ~ batch + tissue") +
    theme_uc()
save_figure(p, "scree", fig_dir, height = 3.5)
p
```

## 2. What the leading component relates to

```{r drivers}
scores <- tibble(line = lines$line, PC1 = pc0$x[, 1], PC2 = pc0$x[, 2]) %>%
    left_join(select(lines, line, tissue, batch, n_injections), by = "line") %>%
    mutate(
        median_log2 = apply(data$log2[line, ], 1, median),
        imputed_ions = rowSums(data$raw[line, ] <= 0)
    )
# correlation of PC1 and PC2 with per-line quantities
sapply(c(median_log2 = "median_log2", n_injections = "n_injections", imputed_ions = "imputed_ions"), function(v)
    round(c(PC1 = cor(scores$PC1, scores[[v]], method = "spearman"),
            PC2 = cor(scores$PC2, scores[[v]], method = "spearman")), 2))
summary(scores$median_log2)
```

```{r drivers-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- ggplot(scores, aes(median_log2, PC1)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Median log2 intensity of the line", y = "Residual PC1",
         title = "Leading residual component vs overall intensity") +
    theme_uc()
save_figure(p, "pc1_vs_median", fig_dir, height = 3.5)
p
```

## 3. Candidate covariates

```{r covariates}
lines_cov <- lines %>%
    mutate(median_log2 = apply(data$log2[line, ], 1, median),
           residual_pc1 = pc0$x[line, 1])
fit_residual <- function(formula) {
    X <- model.matrix(formula, data = lines_cov)
    residuals(limma::lmFit(y, X), y)
}
tibble(
    model = c("~ batch + tissue", "+ median log2 intensity", "+ residual PC1"),
    median_abs_correlation = c(
        median_abs_cor(residual0),
        median_abs_cor(fit_residual(~ batch + tissue + median_log2)),
        median_abs_cor(fit_residual(~ batch + tissue + residual_pc1))
    )
) %>% mutate(median_abs_correlation = round(median_abs_correlation, 3))
```

## 4. Effect on the positive control

```{r positive-control}
# NRF2 in lung lines, as in analysis/05, with and without each covariate
contrast <- config$differential$contrasts$nrf2_lung
d <- contrast_lines(data, contrast, config) %>%
    left_join(select(lines_cov, line, median_log2, residual_pc1), by = "line")

ion_sets <- readr::read_tsv(file.path(derived_dir, "06_ion_sets.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
pc_sets <- config$enrichment$positive_control$sets
glutathione_index <- lapply(setNames(pc_sets, pc_sets), function(s) unique(ion_sets$feature_id[ion_sets$set_source_id == s]))
readout_ions <- data$ions$feature_id[grepl("glutathione", data$ions$name, ignore.case = TRUE)]

check <- function(extra) {
    X <- contrast_design(d, c(contrast$blocking, extra, contrast$covariates))
    # keep the group effect last for contrast_design's convention
    X <- X[, c(setdiff(colnames(X), "groupTRUE"), "groupTRUE")]
    fit <- fit_contrast(data, d, X)
    gsh <- fit$table %>% filter(name == "Glutathione")
    readout <- limma::fry(fit$y, index = list(readouts = readout_ions), design = X, contrast = ncol(X))
    camera <- limma::camera(fit$y, index = glutathione_index, design = X, contrast = ncol(X), inter.gene.cor = NA)
    resid <- residuals(limma::lmFit(fit$y, X), fit$y)
    tibble(covariate = if (length(extra)) extra else "none",
           ions_adj_p_below_0.05 = sum(fit$table$adj.P.Val < 0.05),
           glutathione_logFC = round(gsh$logFC, 2), glutathione_adj_p = signif(gsh$adj.P.Val, 2),
           readout_set_fry_p = signif(readout$PValue, 2),
           camera_hsa00480_p = signif(camera["hsa00480", "PValue"], 2),
           camera_R_HSA_174403_p = signif(camera["R-HSA-174403", "PValue"], 2),
           camera_WP100_p = signif(camera["WP100", "PValue"], 2),
           median_abs_correlation = round(median_abs_cor(resid), 3))
}
bind_rows(check(character()), check("median_log2"), check("residual_pc1"))
```

## 5. What the leading component contains

```{r pc1-content}
loading <- pc0$rotation[, 1]
ions <- data$ions %>% mutate(loading = loading[feature_id], mean_log2 = rowMeans(y)[feature_id])
round(c(loading_vs_mz = cor(ions$loading, ions$ionMz, method = "spearman"),
        loading_vs_mean_intensity = cor(ions$loading, ions$mean_log2, method = "spearman"),
        loading_vs_replicate_signal_ratio = cor(ions$loading, ions$replicate_signal_ratio, method = "spearman")), 2)
ions %>% group_by(metabolite_class) %>%
    summarise(ions = n(), mean_loading = round(mean(loading), 3), share_positive = round(mean(loading > 0), 2),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(ions >= 15) %>% arrange(desc(mean_loading))
ions %>% arrange(desc(loading)) %>% head(10) %>% transmute(name = substr(name, 1, 50), ionMz = round(ionMz), loading = round(loading, 3))
```

## Interpretation

- **There is no global technical factor.** The median intensity of a line
  hardly varies (log2 12.2–12.7, as expected for the authors' normalised
  data), relates only weakly to the leading residual component (Spearman
  0.26), and as a covariate does not lower the correlation between ions
  (0.16 → 0.17). Number of injections and imputed values do not explain it
  either.
- **The residual structure is one strong axis of variation between lines.**
  After batch and tissue, the first component explains 20 % of the residual
  variance, against 3 % in permuted data. It is not a size factor: half of
  the ions load positively, half negatively. The ions that load most are
  phosphatidylglycerols, citrate/isocitrate, glycerophosphoethanolamine and
  nucleotides (92 % of nucleotide ions load positively). Ions with a strong,
  reproducible line-specific signal load more (Spearman 0.56 with the
  replicate signal ratio). This looks like a biological difference between
  lines rather than a technical artefact; which biology it reflects cannot be
  said from these data.
- **Removing the axis is not justified for the analysis.** As a covariate it
  lowers the correlation (0.16 → 0.10) and slightly strengthens the ion-level
  positive control (25 instead of 17 significant ions; glutathione adjusted p
  0.003). But it is estimated from the same data and probably biological, so
  it may remove signal or bias a contrast that relates to it.
- **Correlation is not why the set-level control fails.** With the axis
  removed, camera still finds no glutathione set (p 0.30–0.97), while the four
  glutathione ions as a set remain clearly higher (fry p 0.0014–0.0044 in all
  models). The pathway sets dilute the signal: KEGG glutathione metabolism
  links 24 ions, of which only about half are unambiguous, and most of its
  ions do not change.

**Conclusions:**

1. No covariate is added to the models; the data need no further
   normalisation for this.
2. The correlation between ions is a property of the data, so a set test has
   to account for it: camera is the appropriate test, and ULM, which assumes
   independent ions, overstates significance here. ULM scores can still be
   used to rank sets.
3. The weak set-level result reflects what the sets contain (many unchanged
   and ambiguous ions), not the test.
